Debezium describes itself as 'an open source distributed platform for change data capture'; CDC captures row-level changes made in a database.

Both are open source. Debezium is a dedicated log-based CDC platform. Airbyte is a general data-movement (ELT) platform with a CDC mode for some database sources: Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB, Oracle, SAP HANA and Db2, as listed in the Airbyte docs checked October 2026. Airbyte runs CDC as scheduled syncs rather than a continuous stream. 'Easiest to set up' is the teacher's opinion.

Correct: if the database commit succeeded, the change is in the log and CDC will pick it up even if the app crashed before publishing. This is the dual-write failure Debezium's outbox post describes. If the commit itself failed, there is nothing to capture, which is also correct.
Correct: CDC tools record a log position/offset. Airbyte says it 'keeps track of the current log position between syncs'; Debezium resumes from its recorded offset.

Reading tables row by row (query-based or polling CDC) works only incrementally if each table has a column like LAST_UPDATE_TIMESTAMP. It also misses hard deletes and intermediate updates between polls, and the polling queries add load. That is why log-based CDC is preferred where available.

Right for PostgreSQL: logical decoding decodes the WAL. In MySQL, though, the binary log is not the WAL. It is a separate logical log of change events used for replication and point-in-time recovery, and MySQL writes a whole transaction to it at COMMIT. InnoDB's own write-ahead (redo) log is a different file. CDC tools read the binlog, not the redo log.
precise_version: CDC reads the database's change log: PostgreSQL's WAL via logical decoding, or MySQL's binary log (a replication log separate from InnoDB's redo log).

note: The MySQL and Elasticsearch parts hold. Airbyte's Elasticsearch source supports full refresh only, and MySQL CDC reads the binlog. The MongoDB example is misleading, though. MongoDB exposes its oplog through change streams, and Debezium's MongoDB connector captures changes through change streams rather than iterating collections. The condition is that MongoDB runs as a replica set or sharded cluster: a standalone server has no oplog, and a one-member replica set works.
precise_version: How CDC reads depends on what the database exposes: MySQL's binlog, PostgreSQL's logical decoding and MongoDB's change streams (replica sets only) give a log; stores without one, like Elasticsearch, can only be re-scanned.

CDC resumes from its offset only if the log is still there. Debezium says that after a restart the connector 'continues reading the WAL where it last left off', and a PostgreSQL replication slot retains WAL during the outage, which can fill the disk. MySQL purges binlogs after a retention period. If the connector's position was purged, Debezium fails and needs a new snapshot.

Streaming from the log is much lighter than polling queries. Two caveats: the initial snapshot that most tools run first (Debezium, Airbyte) does full table reads, and a PostgreSQL slot whose consumer is lagging or stopped makes the server retain WAL and catalog rows.

Works, with conditions. MySQL: the replica must have its binlog enabled, with log_replica_updates set so replicated changes are written to it; both are the default in MySQL 8.4. PostgreSQL: logical slots on a standby need PostgreSQL 16 or later; on 15 and earlier, slots exist only on the primary (Debezium docs, checked October 2026).
precise_version: You can usually point CDC at a replica to offload the primary: on MySQL the replica needs log_replica_updates (default on), and on PostgreSQL this needs version 16+.

The contrast holds, but SSE is not 'front-end JavaScript'. It is an HTTP server-push standard: the server sends a text/event-stream response, and EventSource is the browser API that reads it. Both SSE and CDC push changes; SSE pushes from a server to a web page, CDC from a database to another system.

The logs do hold committed transactions in commit order. MySQL writes the whole transaction to the binlog at COMMIT, and PostgreSQL decodes only committed transactions, between begin and commit callbacks. But CDC tools emit one event per row, so the sink does not apply the transaction atomically by default. Debezium can add transaction boundary events with provide.transaction.metadata, which defaults to false.

Correct at the source: PostgreSQL decodes concurrent transactions 'in commit order', and the MySQL binlog is 'logged in commit order'. Downstream ordering is only as strong as the pipeline. Debezium's ordering guarantee is per topic, not across tables, so cross-table order can be lost unless the consumer reorders.

PGSync is a CDC tool that syncs to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch via PostgreSQL logical replication. As of its GitHub README checked 2026-10-13, it also supports MySQL and MariaDB (via the binary log), so 'only works with Postgres' no longer holds.

Correct. Redis wraps allocation in zmalloc, which updates a used_memory counter (zmalloc_used_memory). Redis then compares memory against maxmemory when a client runs a command that adds data, and evicts until it is back under the limit.

Correct: replicas hold the same data, so one CDC reader per source is enough.

For one log stream, only active-standby works. PostgreSQL: 'Only one receiver may consume changes from a slot at any given time', and the Debezium PostgreSQL connector 'always uses a single task'. High availability comes from restarting that task elsewhere. 'All active' works only by splitting the work, for example different tables or databases per connector, each with its own slot and offsets.
precise_version: One log stream has one active reader (with a standby for failover); to run several active CDC instances, give each a separate slice of tables with its own slot/offset.

note: The idea is right: each tool persists its position. The mechanisms differ: Debezium stores offsets in the Kafka Connect offsets topic, and Kafka Connect, not app-level remote locks, decides which worker runs a task. Airbyte stores the log position between syncs.
Correct: background jobs write the database without API events, and log-based CDC still captures those writes.

Depends on the tool. Debezium writes once to Kafka, and any number of sink connectors read those topics. Debezium Server has a single sink type per instance. An Airbyte connection links one source to one destination, so fanning out means several connections, each reading the source (in PostgreSQL, one slot per consumer).
Plausible reasoning: per-sink transformations multiply work and buffering; scale the CDC workers accordingly.
